intrinsic_value_estimate: About $56–76 per share (central ~$60–65). Method: owner earnings (1988 net income to common $1,038M + D&A $170M + deferred tax $44M − undistributed equity income $36M − 1986–88 average capex $345M ≈ $871M, or $2.39/share conservative; ~$2.60 midpoint; $2.88 if maintenance capex ≈ depreciation). Grown 10 years at the company's own record rates (11% for 1978–88 EPS; ~13% constant-currency plus buybacks), valued at 12–15x in year 10, dividends added, discounted at an assumed ~9% long-bond yield. Plus affiliate stakes at carrying value of $5.39/share. Downside case (8% growth, currency reversal, 12x) is ~$46. The framework's literal net-working-capital test fails (NWC $1.06/share); the operative 1987–89 standard is 'an outstanding business at a sensible price'.
margin_of_safety: About 17–39% against the base cases (value $56–76 vs. price $46.56), or about 9–34% without the affiliate stakes. Roughly zero (−2%) in the downside case. Owner-earnings yield is 5.1–6.2% today versus an assumed ~9% bond yield, so the margin depends on owner earnings continuing to grow at the recorded ~11–13% a year, not on assets. That meets the 'sensible price if the past continues' standard (brk-letter-1981#3) but is not the deep 'substantial excess of value' of the generals era. It also fails the literal net-working-capital rule by ~44x.

key_reasons.reason: Not a turnaround, with long demonstrated consistent earning power, so the purchase does not depend on projections.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 2. Filters: turnarounds seldom turn; 1. Berkshire acquisition criteria (demonstrated consistent earning power; future projections are of little interest)
key_reasons.evidence: EPS from continuing operations rose every year from $0.84 (1977) to $2.85 (1988); 27 consecutive dividend increases; 1988 net income $1,044.7M reported 1989-01-31 (ar-1988, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: High return on equity that does not depend on leverage; the core concentrate business earns exceptional returns on its own capital.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (without undue leverage or accounting gimmickry)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE above 20% every year 1978–88, including 1978–81 when debt was 3.8–9.3% of capital; about 25% unlevered return on net capital in 1988; soft-drink segment operating income $1,690.7M on $3,809.0M identifiable assets (~44% pretax), with International at ~64% (ar-1988 notes 15, selected financial data).

key_reasons.reason: Durable, widening moat from the trademark and the global distribution system, with pricing power and low capital needs.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle
key_reasons.evidence: Worldwide share from under 38% (1980) to nearly 45% (1988), more than double the next competitor; US fountain share 59%; gross margin 50.5%→52.6%→55.6% over 1986–88; ~63% gross margin on US concentrate; soft-drink capex $239M vs. $1,691M soft-drink operating income; international per-capita consumption ~51 vs. US ~274 (ar-1986, ar-1987, ar-1988).

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings, so the earnings figure is real cash available to owners.
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 owner earnings ≈ $871M ($2.39/share) on a conservative basis and up to ~$1,049M ($2.88) if maintenance capex ≈ depreciation, versus reported $2.85 EPS; operating cash flow $1,166.8M; capex $386.8M vs. depreciation $167M (ar-1988 cash flow statement).

key_reasons.reason: Management in place has returned large amounts of capital through buybacks and retreated from non-core ventures. Retained earnings have created far more than $1 of market value per $1.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Buybacks only well below intrinsic value; Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value; Honest, able management already in place
key_reasons.evidence: ~69.5M shares repurchased for ~$2.19B over 1984–88 (avg. shares 396M→364.6M); 1981–88 retained $6.46/share vs. market gain $33.50/share (~$5.2 per $1; ~$2.6 at constant P/E); entertainment moved into a 49% affiliate, with $545M in notes repaid in cash in January 1988; coffee sold January 1989 (ar-1987, ar-1988).

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible for an outstanding business if the past simply continues. No catalyst is needed because compounding business value will eventually be reflected in the price.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 5. Valuation (as superseded in practice by 'outstanding business at a sensible price', brk-letter-1987#18 and brk-letter-1981#3); 6. No catalyst needed
key_reasons.evidence: Price $46.56 = 16.3x 1988 EPS and ~17.9x midpoint owner earnings, below the 1987 peak of ~22x; value ~$56–76/share with an 11–13% growth record; 14.4M shares still authorized for repurchase (prices, ar-1988).

key_reasons.reason: Concentrated but below-maximum sizing: the moat makes drastic loss of value unlikely, but the moderate margin of safety and currency exposure fall short of 'extremely high probability' on every fact.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 7. Concentrate when the facts are clear (up to 40%)
key_reasons.evidence: About 76% of operating income from outside the US with 10–27% annual currency tailwinds in 1986–88; downside valuation ~$46 ≈ price; proxy, capex split and Berkshire's current capital are not in the packet.

risks: Currency reversal: ~76% of operating income is international, and a weaker dollar flattered 1986–88 growth (key currencies +27%, +16%, +10%); constant-currency growth is perhaps ~10%.
The margin of safety is moderate and vanishes if growth slows to ~8% and the multiple falls to ~12x; the purchase depends on the moat holding, not on assets.
Elective leverage: total debt / total capital 38.8% (1988), 48.4% (1987); buybacks are partly debt-funded under a 35% net-debt ceiling.

Capital going into low-return bottler stakes (CCE earns ~8% on net assets; $1.9B in affiliates produced $48M equity income in 1988) and the risk of another move outside the core, as with entertainment in 1982–87.
Advertising cost of keeping the moat ($842M media in 1988, up from $513M in 1984) and intense US competition, with efficiency gains passed to retail prices.
Hyperinflation and economic instability in Latin American markets (Brazil, Argentina volume and income declines in 1988).
Accounting latitude: discretionary concentrate pricing to the 49%-owned CCE and frequent restatements; FASB 96 may cut equity ~$175M; Puerto Rico tax exemption expires in 1995.
Compensation is not tied to return on capital: 1988 option grants of 4.18M (vs. 1.1–1.8M earlier) and new change-of-control vesting on restricted stock.
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that most capex above depreciation is maintenance, not growth (owner earnings nearer $2.0–2.3), or that bottler investments are a permanent annual cost.
Constant-currency results showing underlying growth well below ~10% a year.
A long-bond yield well above the assumed ~9%, which would remove the margin of safety at this price.
Proxy or meeting evidence that management sees buybacks only as cash disposal, without regard to price versus value, or plans large acquisitions outside soft drinks.
Insider/director ownership negligible, or compensation clearly rewarding size over per-share returns.
Upside: a price drop back to the 1988 range ($35–40) would widen the margin of safety and justify sizing toward the 40% cap.
sell_triggers: Sustained loss of worldwide or US share to the main competitor, i.e. the moat narrowing rather than widening.
Gross or concentrate margins falling persistently, showing lost pricing power.
Major capital deployed outside the soft-drink core (a repeat of the entertainment diversification) at returns below the cost of capital.
Issuing shares below intrinsic value, or pushing leverage materially beyond the stated 35% net-debt ceiling to support EPS.
Evidence that management is not candid, e.g. reported figures materially misrepresenting the economics, or hidden liabilities in the bottler system.
Not a trigger: a high market price alone. A great business with good managers is held as a permanent holding (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1983#2).
